metadata.name: Provenance Guard frozen development inputs
metadata.publication_year_definition: Year of the original work's first publication, rather than the date of digitization or the linked source edition.
metadata.normalization: Human excerpts preserve source wording and punctuation; printed line breaks and paragraph breaks are collapsed to spaces. Edition footnote markers are retained when present.
metadata.selection: Opening literary and first-person passages, plus formal nonfiction, selected before scoring. No passage was selected based on a detector result.
metadata.limits: A small development sample, not an independent attack set or a representative benchmark. Human passages are historical published writing, not the submitter's original writing. AI passages are generated by Codex; detector outcomes cannot establish authorship. Calibration items are demonstrations and are excluded from the fixed 10-human/4-AI metric groups.

human.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife. However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.
human.author: Jane Austen
human.title: Pride and Prejudice
human.provenance: Exact public-domain excerpt from the Project Gutenberg edition of Austen's published novel, verified against the linked primary text on 2026-10-30. Whitespace normalized.

human.text: There was no possibility of taking a walk that day. We had been wandering, indeed, in the leafless shrubbery an hour in the morning; but since dinner (Mrs. Reed, when there was no company, dined early) the cold winter wind had brought with it clouds so sombre, and a rain so penetrating, that further outdoor exercise was now out of the question. I was glad of it: I never liked long walks, especially on chilly afternoons: dreadful to me was the coming home in the raw twilight, with nipped fingers and toes, and a heart saddened by the chidings of Bessie, the nurse, and humbled by the consciousness of my physical inferiority to Eliza, John, and Georgiana Reed.
human.author: Charlotte Brontë
human.title: Jane Eyre: An Autobiography
human.provenance: Exact public-domain excerpt from the Project Gutenberg edition of Brontë's published novel, verified against the linked primary text on 2026-10-30. Whitespace normalized.

human.text: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world. It is a way I have of driving off the spleen and regulating the circulation. Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and methodically knocking people’s hats off—then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can.
human.author: Herman Melville
human.title: Moby Dick; Or, The Whale
human.location: Chapter 1, Loomings, opening through 'as soon as I can.'
human.provenance: Exact public-domain excerpt from the Project Gutenberg edition of Melville's published novel, verified against the linked primary text on 2026-10-30. Whitespace normalized.

human.text: You don’t know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain’t no matter. That book was made by Mr. Mark Twain, and he told the truth, mainly. There was things which he stretched, but mainly he told the truth. That is nothing. I never seen anybody but lied one time or another, without it was Aunt Polly, or the widow, or maybe Mary. Aunt Polly—Tom’s Aunt Polly, she is—and Mary, and the Widow Douglas is all told about in that book, which is mostly a true book, with some stretchers, as I said before.
human.author: Mark Twain
human.title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
human.provenance: Exact public-domain excerpt from the Project Gutenberg edition of Twain's published novel, verified against the linked primary text on 2026-10-30. Whitespace normalized. First UK publication was 1884; US publication followed in 1885.

human.text: When I wrote the following pages, or rather the bulk of them, I lived alone, in the woods, a mile from any neighbor, in a house which I had built myself, on the shore of Walden Pond, in Concord, Massachusetts, and earned my living by the labor of my hands only. I lived there two years and two months. At present I am a sojourner in civilized life again.
human.author: Henry David Thoreau
human.title: Walden
human.provenance: Exact public-domain excerpt from Walden in the Project Gutenberg volume Walden, and On The Duty Of Civil Disobedience, verified against the linked primary text on 2026-10-30. Whitespace normalized.

human.text: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings. I arrived here yesterday, and my first task is to assure my dear sister of my welfare and increasing confidence in the success of my undertaking. I am already far north of London, and as I walk in the streets of Petersburgh, I feel a cold northern breeze play upon my cheeks, which braces my nerves and fills me with delight. Do you understand this feeling?
human.author: Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley
human.title: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
human.location: Letter 1, opening through 'Do you understand this feeling?'

The work first appeared in 1818 and was revised in 1831; this is a transcription from the linked edition, not a claim that it is the 1818 wording. Whitespace normalized.

human.text: Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do: once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it, “and what is the use of a book,” thought Alice “without pictures or conversations?” So she was considering in her own mind (as well as she could, for the hot day made her feel very sleepy and stupid), whether the pleasure of making a daisy-chain would be worth the trouble of getting up and picking the daisies, when suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran close by her.
human.author: Lewis Carroll
human.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
human.location: Chapter I, Down the Rabbit-Hole, first two paragraphs

human.text: When on board H.M.S. ‘Beagle,’ as naturalist, I was much struck with certain facts in the distribution of the inhabitants of South America, and in the geological relations of the present to the past inhabitants of that continent. These facts seemed to me to throw some light on the origin of species—that mystery of mysteries, as it has been called by one of our greatest philosophers. On my return home, it occurred to me, in 1837, that something might perhaps be made out on this question by patiently accumulating and reflecting on all sorts of facts which could possibly have any bearing on it.
human.author: Charles Darwin
human.title: On the Origin of Species By Means of Natural Selection
human.provenance: Exact public-domain excerpt from the Project Gutenberg edition of Darwin's published work, verified against the linked primary text on 2026-10-30. Whitespace normalized.

human.text: The produce of industry is what it adds to the subject or materials upon which it is employed. In proportion as the value of this produce is great or small, so will likewise be the profits of the employer. But it is only for the sake of profit that any man employs a capital in the support of industry; and he will always, therefore, endeavour to employ it in the support of that industry of which the produce is likely to be of the greatest value, or to exchange for the greatest quantity either of money or of other goods.
human.author: Adam Smith
human.title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
human.location: Book IV, Chapter II, paragraph beginning 'The produce of industry'
human.provenance: Exact public-domain excerpt from the Project Gutenberg edition of Smith's published work, verified against the linked primary text on 2026-10-30. Whitespace normalized.

human.text: My elder brothers were all put apprentices to different trades. I was put to the grammar-school at eight years of age, my father intending to devote me, as the tithe[13] of his sons, to the service of the Church. My early readiness in learning to read (which must have been very early, as I do not remember when I could not read), and the opinion of all his friends, that I should certainly make a good scholar, encouraged him in this purpose of his. My uncle Benjamin, too, approved of it, and proposed to give me all his short-hand volumes of sermons, I suppose as a stock to set up with, if I would learn his character.[14]
human.author: Benjamin Franklin
human.title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
human.location: Passage beginning 'My elder brothers were all put apprentices', first four sentences
human.provenance: Exact public-domain excerpt from the Project Gutenberg transcription of the 1916 English edition (1922 printing), verified against the linked primary text on 2026-10-30. The memoir was composed in 1771–1790 and initially published in French in 1791. The linked edition states that its text follows Bigelow's nineteenth-century editions. Edition footnote markers retained; whitespace normalized.

ai.text: Effective communication is essential for building a productive and collaborative workplace. By establishing clear expectations and encouraging open dialogue, organizations can ensure that every team member understands their responsibilities. Regular feedback helps employees identify opportunities for improvement while reinforcing successful habits. In addition, consistent documentation allows important information to remain accessible as projects evolve. Managers should create an environment where questions are welcomed and different perspectives are respected. This approach supports accountability, reduces misunderstandings, and strengthens trust across departments. Ultimately, investing in thoughtful communication practices enables teams to work more efficiently and achieve sustainable results together.
ai.provenance: Generated before detector evaluation on 2026-10-30. Original synthetic workplace advice; not independently human-authored or copied from a source.
ai.generation_prompt: Write a polished, approximately 100-word paragraph of ordinary workplace communication advice.

ai.text: A successful morning routine begins with a clear and achievable plan. Start by choosing a consistent time to wake up each day. Next, drink a glass of water and prepare a simple breakfast. Set aside a few minutes to review your most important tasks. Keep your workspace organized so that necessary materials are easy to find. Limit unnecessary notifications during periods that require your full attention. Take short breaks to maintain focus and prevent mental fatigue. Review your progress at the end of each working session. Small, consistent improvements can make daily responsibilities easier to manage over time.
ai.provenance: Generated before detector evaluation on 2026-10-30. Original synthetic routine advice with deliberately regular sentence structure.
ai.generation_prompt: Write approximately 100 words of routine advice using plain sentences of fairly consistent length.

ai.text: Rain gardens provide a practical way to manage stormwater while supporting healthy urban environments. These shallow planted areas collect runoff from roofs, sidewalks, and driveways, allowing water to soak gradually into the ground. Native plants help stabilize the soil and provide food and shelter for local wildlife. Because rain gardens slow the movement of water, they can also reduce the amount of sediment reaching nearby streams. Successful installation requires attention to drainage, soil conditions, and the distance from building foundations. With appropriate planning and routine maintenance, a rain garden can become an attractive and useful feature of a neighborhood.
ai.provenance: Generated before detector evaluation on 2026-10-30. Original synthetic general explainer; not a sourced human passage.
ai.generation_prompt: Write an approximately 100-word informational paragraph explaining rain gardens in a polished general-audience style.
